# Solutions and Solubility

## Core ideas and reasoning

A solution contains solute dispersed in a solvent. A saturated solution is in equilibrium with undissolved solute at a specified temperature; solubility commonly means grams of solute per 100 g solvent at that temperature. It is not the same as grams per 100 g solution. Many solids become more soluble as temperature rises, but not all; read the supplied curve rather than assume. Cooling a saturated solution may crystallise excess solute. Calculate the amount remaining dissolved at the new temperature using the same mass of solvent. Concentration may be expressed in g dm⁻³ or mol dm⁻³; convert using molar mass. Dilution adds solvent without changing solute moles, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ when no reaction or loss occurs. Dissolving faster through stirring does not necessarily increase equilibrium solubility. Gas solubility often decreases with temperature and increases with gas pressure. Keep temperature and solvent quantity explicit in comparisons.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

A salt has solubility 40 g per 100 g water at 60°C and 25 g at 20°C. How much crystallises from a saturated solution containing 100 g water on cooling?

Initially 40 g is dissolved. At 20°C only 25 g remains dissolved, so 40 - 25 = 15 g crystallises, assuming no water loss.

### Example 2

What volume of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ solution is needed to prepare 250 cm³ of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ solution?

c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ gives V₁ = 0.20 × 250/2.0 = 25 cm³. Dilute this to a final volume of 250 cm³.

### Example 3

Convert 4.0 g dm⁻³ NaOH to mol dm⁻³. Use NaOH molar mass 40 g mol⁻¹.

4.0/40 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³. Each mole contributes 40 g, so the reverse conversion gives 4.0 g dm⁻³.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
